stops.name: Smyrna, the brawl in the port
stops.campa: Working his way toward Egypt, he lands in Smyrna and is baptized into the fraternity of ports: a night quarrel among sailors becomes a general battle, and he wakes bruised beside new friends from a foreign fleet. The fists buy him what money could not: passage. He ships as a hand toward Alexandria, one more dark-eyed young man among the rigging, with the copied map of drowned-in-sand Egypt strapped under his shirt and a purpose no one on board could guess.

stops.name: Giza, the Sphinx, and the meeting at its paws
stops.campa: He works as a guide among the pyramids, spending his nights comparing the stones against the parchment of pre-sand Egypt. Sitting at the foot of the Sphinx, absorbed in the map, he is found by a Russian archaeologist, Professor Skridlov, and then by the man whose life will braid with his for thirty-five years: Prince Yuri Lubovedsky, who sees the map and turns pale, for he has been hunting the same trail. Guide and prince recognize each other as seekers. Egypt gives him no final answer, but it gives him his brotherhood; together they will go up the Nile to Thebes and sit among the tombs.

stops.name: Jerusalem: guide at the Holy Sepulchre
stops.campa: He earns his bread as a guide to Russian pilgrims in Jerusalem, leading peasants who have walked half a continent to kiss the Stone of Unction. He learns the city as a professional of holiness: the Easter fire, the rival monks policing inches of the Sepulchre, the trade in relics; and he studies faith itself as a force: what it does in a body, what it heals, what it blinds. The Essenes enter his research here; he will say later that among their heirs certain psalms were made to grow plants faster. The seeker files Jerusalem among the places where truth once stood and left a forwarding address.

stops.name: Crete, the first stray bullet
stops.campa: Insurrection burns across Crete, and he is on the island, the canon says on a political errand among the Greeks, when the first of his three stray bullets finds him, in the year before the Greco-Turkish war. He falls without seeing who fired. Unknown Greeks carry his unconscious body off the island, and he wakes far away, in Jerusalem, mended by strangers. It is the first of the three woundings, each of which will drop him at the door of death and each time send him back changed, as if the bullets themselves were part of the curriculum.

stops.name: Mecca and Medina, the hajj in disguise
stops.campa: Dressed and bearded as a pilgrim, speaking the tongues he has collected like keys, he enters the forbidden cities where an unmasked unbeliever dies. He circles the Kaaba in the white flood of the hajj, stands at Medina, watches everything with the double sight of the seeker. And he concludes what he concluded at Echmiadzin and Jerusalem: the secret is not here either; the outer rite guards an emptied room. Whatever Islam keeps of the old knowledge, he decides, is kept elsewhere: in Bokhara, among the dervish orders of the east. The needle of the search swings toward Turkestan.

stops.name: Bokhara, the reservoir of the dervishes
stops.campa: Bokhara the Noble: a hundred madrasahs, the last emirate where the muezzin's law still runs, and beneath the official piety a web of dervish lineages older than the mosques. He comes with Soloviev, the ex-drunkard he cured and converted into a brother of the search, and they burrow into the city's underlife: Sufi zikr, the science of breath, the mathematics of music. Here the trail of the Sarmoung, first read on parchment at Ani, grows warm at last: contact is made, a promise given. They wait for the guides the brotherhood will send.

stops.name: The Amu Darya crossing
stops.campa: At dawn they are put onto the great river the ancients called Oxus, the water that has carried armies, prophets and smuggled knowledge for three thousand years. The ferry crawls; the yellow current tugs at the poles; on the far bank Asia deepens and the writ of every empire thins. The canon keeps this river as a threshold: beyond the Amu Darya begin the roads that do not appear on Russian maps, and the two travelers cross it the way other men cross into a church.

stops.name: The Sarmoung Monastery, the blindfolded journey; the dances read as books
stops.campa: Four Kara-Kirghiz guides come; the condition is a vow: hoods over the eyes. Twelve days on horseback through passes, the blindfolds lifted only at rope bridges swaying over gorges. Then a valley no map names, courtyards, silence: the Sarmoung, unbroken since Babylon. In the third court the priestess-dancers work before apparatuses like branching trees strung with ivory pegs: each peg-posture a letter, each dance a book, truths written in movement, copied for millennia. In a corridor he meets, white-haired, Prince Lubovedsky; the brotherhood gathered him too. What he carries out of this valley becomes the Movements; every sacred dance he will stage is a page from this library.
stops.quote: In the strictly defined movements and combinations of the dancers, certain laws are visually reproduced which are intelligible to those who know them. Such dances are called sacred dances.
stops.quote_source: In Search of the Miraculous (Ouspensky), ch. I: Gurdjieff on the temple dances of the east

stops.name: The Gobi, stilts against the sand-wind; the death of Soloviev
stops.campa: The Seekers of Truth, full expedition now (professors, engineers, the indestructible Vitvitskaia), strike into the sands to find a city the legends say lies under the Gobi. Against the sand-wind they engineer stilts, planning to walk above the killing layer of blown grit; the sheep that carry their supplies are to become raft and provisions in turn. In the desert's outer scrub a wild camel bites Soloviev; he dies within hours, and they bury the cured drunkard, the truest of brothers, in sand that has no address. The expedition turns back. The desert keeps its city and takes its fee.

stops.name: Lhasa, the Tibetan years and the second bullet
stops.campa: The legend gives him years on the roof of the world: Lhasa before the British guns, monasteries where he studies the technique of the lamas, a Tibetan marriage, whispers that the Russian agent the British files call the shadowy Buriat is partly him. In 1902, in the mountains, the second stray bullet drops him, again from a quarrel that was not his. Comrades pack his body through the passes and he lies for months at the edge of consciousness beside one of the great Central Asian deserts, nursed back by wind and goat's milk, while armies gather below to break open the country he is leaving.

stops.name: Chiatura, the third bullet, and the ledge above the abyss
stops.campa: Back in the Caucasus in the year of revolutions, near the Chiatura tunnel, he walks into crossfire between Cossacks and Gurian rebels, and the third stray bullet finds him as the fortune-teller of Alexandropol promised. Friends smuggle the bleeding man across half of Asia to the oasis of Yangi Hissar on the rim of the Takla-makan, where he convalesces in the long silence of the desert's edge. There, the canon says, he holds the great review of his life: three bullets, three resurrections. Chance is dismissed as an explanation. Something is either guarding him or collecting on him, and he resolves to find out which.

stops.name: Tashkent, the professional hypnotist, and the oath
stops.campa: He sets up in Tashkent as healer, hypnotist, professor of supernatural sciences: curing drunkards and opium-eaters, staging wonders for the colonial parlors, and all the while running his true experiment: the mapping of human suggestibility, the mechanics of the sleep men call waking life. Money pours in; he becomes rich as a fish in water among the credulous. Then, in the autumn of 1911, he stops. He swears the great oath before his own essence: an artificial life, planned in advance, and his hypnotic power never again for his own profit. The magician binds himself, and the teacher becomes possible.
stops.quote: According to the special oath I took, I bound myself in my conscience to lead in some ways an artificial life, modelled upon a programme which had been previously planned in accordance with certain definite principles.
stops.quote_source: The Herald of Coming Good (the special oath of the artificial life, as Gurdjieff recounts it)
